newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexican markets skittish on U.S. drug vote.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexican markets skittish on U.S. drug vote.

text.p: Mexican financial markets held their collective breath on Thursday ahead of a key U.S. congressional vote on Mexico's anti-drug efforts -- a decision seen here as a vote of confidence in Mexico itself.

Mexico's main stock index was off 16 points, or 0.43 percent at 3,742 points at 1225 local time (1825 GMT) and the peso had slipped 3.6 centavos to 8.001/8.006 per dollar in widely-watched 48-hour contracts.
Secondary interest rates on overnight T-bills, or Cetes, were also 15 basis points higher at 23.15 percent.
Traders said worries about a U.S. House of Representatives vote later on Thursday on whether or not to "certify" Mexico as an anti-drug ally was a key factor.
The House vote was due mid-afternoon Thursday.
"The whole (certification) process seems to be unnerving," Lars Schonander, chief analyst for Santander Investments in Mexico City, told Reuters.

"It's very definitely negative for the markets. Even if you get decertification without (economic) penalites, it'll still negatively affect perceptions of Mexico even though there is no real economic or financial impact."

"They're nervous and they're selling. The Dow plunged on U.S. economic data and the only thing holding us back is the bourse's traditional slow start and cold feet over the decertification vote," said one stock market trader.

Dealers said the sell-off had not been worse because some investors were betting that the U.S. representatives would not risk censuring Mexico, which has vowed to retaliate if it does not win the congressional seal of drug approval.
"I don't think they'll go ahead with it, they are just telling us to get our house in order with all the scandals that we've had," said another stock market trader.
Mexican and U.S. officials have said that a negative vote could spark a political backlash in Mexico and hit its financial markets by undermining foreign investor sentiment.
"Decertification = Instability" screamed the banner headline of Mexico's El Financiero newspaper on Thursday.

U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers told U.S. senators on Wednesday that a decision to strip Mexico of its anti-drug certification could cause pressure on the peso, raise interest rates and hurt investment.
